analysis.one_liner: Tightens oil spill prevention rules for single-hull tankers and speeds compensation for people hurt by spills.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 1996, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 to strengthen spill prevention: safety equipment and operating rules for single-hull tankers and barges, deadlines that turn stalled proposed Coast Guard rules into final rules, and loss of liability caps when a spill is caused by breaking safety regulations. It also would have let spill victims claim interim payments for lost income without giving up the rest of their claim, required advance planning for closing and reopening fishing grounds after a spill, and made up to $50 million a year from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund available for assessing damage and starting restoration. It never got past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishermen, and tourism and seafood businesses that lose income when a spill closes waters: the bill would have guaranteed access to interim, short-term compensation without waiving later claims, required prompt science-based decisions on reopening fishing grounds, and funded ecological mitigation from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund. Crew members on aging single-hull vessels would also have gained from the safety requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fishermen and coastal communities hurt by spills

how_it_helps.text: If the Coast Guard failed to finalize proposed rules on single-hull tanker operations by set deadlines, the proposed rules would automatically take effect as final rules, covering operational and structural standards for tank vessels over 5,000 gross tons without double hulls [S2][S3].

Single-hull barges over 5,000 gross tons in open ocean or coastal waters would need crew aboard with an operable anchor, an emergency tow-line retrieval system, or a comparable anti-grounding measure, and ports would set minimum under-keel clearances for vessels without double bottoms [S2][S3].

Spill victims claiming lost profits or earning capacity could recover partial, interim damages, and accepting a short-term payment would not bar later recovery of the remaining damages; claims advertisements would have to say so [S2][S3].

The President would have to issue guidance so Area Committees can plan in advance for closing and reopening fishing grounds after a spill, and Area Contingency Plans would compile lists of local scientific experts who could be convened immediately in response to a spill [S2][S3].

Up to $50 million per fiscal year from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund could go to natural resource damage assessments, restoration plan development, and initial restoration implementation, and the Fund could pay costs to mitigate ecological injury [S2][S3].
Liability limits would no longer apply when a spill from a double-hulled vessel was proximately caused by a violation of a federal safety, construction, or operating regulation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tank vessel and barge operators, which face new equipment and operating requirements and, when a spill is caused by violating safety rules, uncapped liability; oil cargo owners, who are the responsible parties under the Oil Pollution Act and can be passed these costs. Some of that cost flows into shipping rates and ultimately oil prices, and the Trust Fund draws would come from industry-funded fees rather than general taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would make proposed rules automatically effective as final rules when deadlines pass, sidestepping the normal process of finalizing regulations after public comment [S3].

New equipment, fire-suppression, and operating requirements impose compliance costs on towing vessels and single-hull tankers and barges, which the industry can pass through to shippers and consumers [S2][S3].

Removing liability caps when a violation causes a spill exposes vessel owners and their insurers to potentially unlimited damages, a cost that honest supporters would acknowledge and that the industry strongly resists generally [S2][S3].
The bill adds studies, planning protocols, scientific support teams, and information clearinghouses, all of which carry administrative costs [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but modest and regional: better prevention on aging single-hull vessels, faster compensation for spilled-on businesses, and quicker reopening of fishing grounds all address problems the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill and the 1990 law left unresolved. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and are partly passed to consumers in oil transport prices. On balance the benefits to coastal communities outweigh the compliance costs, though the automatic-final-rule mechanism is a blunt way to force agency action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then two of its subcommittees for the rest of the 104th Congress, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1997 without any vote ever being scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on June 4, 1996, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
On June 17, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of single-hull tank vessels and barges, and the oil shipping industry generally, avoided new prevention requirements and the threat of uncapped liability. Coastal communities and fishermen who lose income to spills got no help.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Single-hull oil tanker and barge operators

for.name: Rep. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Bud Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to two subcommittees and never took it up for consideration; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members put their names on the bill, one Democrat and one Republican, and no votes ever occurred, so no partisan split on the merits can be measured.

industries.industry: Tank vessel operators (oil tankers and barges)
industries.note: The bill imposes equipment, fire-suppression, and operating requirements on single-hull vessels and barges, forces stalled proposed rules into effect by deadline, and removes liability caps when a violation causes a spill. The industry profits from operating older single-hull tonnage, so its interest in this bill runs against cheaper, less-regulated operations.

Required advance planning for closing and reopening fishing grounds, interim damage payments for lost profits, and funded ecological mitigation all shorten the time fishing families and seafood businesses go uncompensated after a spill.
As responsible parties under the Oil Pollution Act, oil cargo owners ultimately bear spill liability and would face higher transport costs as stricter prevention rules raise shipping prices.
